Question: Several sets of prime numbers, such as \(\{7, 83, 421, 659\},\) use each of the nine nonzero digits exactly once. What is the smallest possible sum such a set of primes could have?
Solution:
To minimize the sum, we want digits in low place values. The restriction that every number is prime forces some digits into higher positions.

The only even prime is \(2\), so none of the digits \(4,6,8\) can be the units digit of a prime, including a one-digit prime. Each must therefore occupy a tens or higher position, contributing at least ten times its face value.

The sum of all nine digit values is \(1+2+\cdots+9=45\). Every digit contributes at least its face value, and the digits \(4,6,8\) contribute at least nine additional copies of their values. If \(S\) is the sum of the primes, then
\[
S\ge45+9(4+6+8)=207.
\]
Higher positions can only increase these contributions, so this bound applies to every allowed set.

The set
\[
\{2,5,7,43,61,89\}
\]
uses each nonzero digit exactly once and sums to \(207\). Its entries are prime: the three two-digit entries are below \(100\) and have no prime divisor among \(2,3,5,7\), the only possible prime divisors below \(10\). Thus the bound is attained, and the smallest sum is \(\boxed{207}\), choice B.
